featured.title: Digital SME
featured.tagline: A retrieval-grounded support assistant that answers from your own runbooks instead of guessing.
featured.problem: Enterprise support teams held their knowledge in scattered runbooks, ticket history and the heads of a handful of senior engineers. New joiners escalated problems that had already been solved a dozen times, and a general-purpose LLM was worse than useless here: it answered confidently from training data that had never seen the customer's environment.
approach: Ground every answer in retrieved internal documents, never in model memory alone.
Return citations with each answer so an engineer can verify before acting.
Keep the retrieval corpus and the model swappable, so neither becomes a lock-in point.

decisions.title: RAG over fine-tuning
decisions.chose: Retrieval-augmented generation against a live document corpus
decisions.why: Support knowledge changes weekly. Retrieval lets the corpus update without a training cycle, and every answer carries a citation an engineer can check.
decisions.rejected: Fine-tuning a base model — slow to update, expensive to re-run, and it makes hallucinations harder to trace back to a source.

decisions.title: Cloud Run over GKE
decisions.why: Support traffic is bursty and follows business hours. Paying for idle nodes overnight buys nothing, and the team should not be operating a control plane to serve a chatbot.
decisions.rejected: A GKE cluster — right answer at a much larger scale, wrong answer for the operational burden it adds today.

decisions.title: Citations as a product requirement
decisions.chose: Every response renders its source documents inline
decisions.why: In support, an unverifiable answer is a liability. Citations turn the assistant from an oracle into a research tool, which is what actually earns engineer trust.
decisions.rejected: A cleaner chat-only UI — better looking, but it hides exactly the information that makes the output usable.

outcomes: Projected impact: 20% support-productivity gain and 10% reduction in consult rates via query deflection and high-accuracy guidance.
High-risk customers are flagged pre-escalation from historical signals — escalation rate, CES, stagnation.
Support knowledge is queryable in natural language instead of grep-and-hope across runbooks, with sources attached to every answer.
New joiners self-serve on problems that previously required a senior escalation.

featured.title: C.O.R.E Assessment Platform
featured.tagline: Adaptive technical assessment with real sandboxed execution — candidates run code, not multiple choice about code.
featured.problem: Multiple-choice tests measure recall, not engineering ability. Assessing whether someone can actually operate a Linux box or debug a Python service means letting them touch a real one — which means running untrusted candidate code, safely, at speed, without letting it reach anything that matters.
approach: Give every candidate a disposable, network-restricted execution sandbox.
Adapt question difficulty from live performance instead of fixing a static paper.
Score behaviour — approach, iteration, recovery — alongside the final answer.

decisions.title: Isolation boundary per candidate
decisions.chose: One ephemeral container per session, no shared runtime, egress denied by default, hard TTL
decisions.why: Candidate code is untrusted by definition. The blast radius of a hostile submission has to end at a container that is thrown away minutes later.
decisions.rejected: A shared multi-tenant runtime with a language-level sandbox — cheaper, but one escape compromises every concurrent session.

decisions.title: Adaptive difficulty over a fixed paper
decisions.chose: Question selection driven by live response signal
decisions.why: A fixed paper wastes a strong candidate's time on warm-ups and buries a weak one. Adapting reaches a confident signal in fewer questions.
decisions.rejected: Static question sets — trivially easier to build and to compare across candidates, at the cost of resolution where it matters.

decisions.title: Behavioural analytics as a first-class signal
decisions.chose: Capture the path to the answer, not just the answer
decisions.why: How someone recovers from a failing command is more predictive than whether they eventually got it right. That signal only exists if you instrument for it from the start.
decisions.rejected: Pass/fail scoring — simple and legible, but it discards the most interesting evidence in the session.

outcomes: Projected impact: 60% improvement in quality hiring and 35% advancement in critical metrics for Cloud Support.
Candidates are assessed on live Linux, Java and Python environments rather than on questions about them.
Untrusted code runs inside a per-session boundary that is disposed on completion.
Assessment reports are generated from behavioral data, not just final scores.

featured.title: Hari.dev
featured.tagline: This site. Zero dependencies, zero build step, JSON-driven content — because the portfolio should demonstrate the claim, not just make it.
featured.problem: A Cloud Architect claiming to care about product quality has a credibility problem: the claim is unfalsifiable unless something in reach of the reader demonstrates it. The portfolio is the one artifact a hiring manager can open DevTools on.
approach: No framework, no bundler, no dependencies — the whole site is auditable in one sitting.
Content lives in JSON and renders through small, single-purpose classes.
Accessibility and performance treated as requirements, not as a later pass.

decisions.title: No framework
decisions.chose: Vanilla JavaScript with ES classes and native APIs
decisions.why: The site has three interactive behaviours. A framework would add a build step, a dependency tree and a supply-chain surface to solve a problem this site does not have.
decisions.rejected: React or Astro — genuinely better past a certain complexity threshold, which this site is nowhere near.

decisions.title: createElement over innerHTML
decisions.why: Template-string rendering interpolates data straight into markup. Even with a trusted corpus, it is the wrong habit to demonstrate on a page whose whole argument is engineering care.
decisions.rejected: Template literals — far more readable, and exactly the pattern that becomes an injection bug the moment content stops being first-party.

decisions.title: JSON-driven content
decisions.chose: Separate data from presentation from the first commit
decisions.why: Adding a role or a case study should be a data edit, not a markup edit. It also makes the content portable to a real CMS or API later without touching the render layer.
decisions.rejected: Hardcoded HTML — faster to ship once, then a maintenance tax on every subsequent change.

outcomes: Ships with no runtime dependencies and no build pipeline.
Keyboard navigable end to end, with reduced-motion and focus-visible support.
Responsive images and system fonts keep the payload small on mobile networks.
